newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Tenaga's Bakun dam stake cut welcomed.
newsitem.headline: Tenaga's Bakun dam stake cut welcomed.

text.p: Investors turned more bullish on Malaysian power utility Tenaga Nasional Bhd on news it had sharply cut its stake in the Bakun hydro-electric dam holding company, analysts said on Thursday.

The government's Economic Planning Unit recently revised the equity ownership structure of the Bakun Hydro-Electric Corp Bhd (BHEC), the holding for the $5.5 billion dam in Sarawak state on Borneo island.
The changes resulted in Tenaga's equity share dropping from 25 percent to five percent.
On Wednesday, following the stake reduction news, Tenaga's stock moved up 55 cents ($0.22), before retracing the gains.

The company unexpectedly said on Wednesday that it would compensate consumers for an August 3 power blackout, but analysts say the payout was insignificant and should not mar the more positive outlook for the utility.
Shares closed unchanged at 9.30 ringgit after the announcement that Tenaga would give 10 percent rebates to 4.2 million consumers for a total of 70 million ringgit.
Malaysian government officials had said earlier that Tenaga may not have to compensate the affected consumers, noting there was no precedent in other countries for such actions.
Tenaga's stock recouped on Thursday, and was up 10 cents at 9.40 ringgit at midday.
"It (the stake cut) is good news for Tenaga, as they have so many more important things to spend their money on than the Bakun project," said an analyst at a local firm.
"For example, Tenaga is going to have to spend around four billion ringgit on upgrading its power transmission system over the next four years," he added.
Tenaga is also going to have to pay heavily for buying power from independent power producers to supplement its own generation capabilities, the analyst said.
The 2,400 MW capacity dam, which has been the target of protests and environmental scrutiny, is expected to be completed in 2002, with power being generated soon after that.
Since Tenaga is going to see returns on its investments only after that time, most analysts taking a shorter-term view see the reduced stake in the project as more of a help than a hindrance.

On the other hand, the rebate issue is seen as less vital. "A compensation amount of about 50 million ringgit would only amount to around five percent of Tenaga's net earnings for 1997, so it would not affect them that much," said Azman Mokhtar, power analyst at UBS Securities in Kuala Lumpur.
Azman was indifferent over the stake that Tenaga has been left with in the Bakun project. "Five percent is neither here nor there," he said.
"The 25 percent would have cost them around 680 million ringgit, which they would only have had to pay over a six to seven year period. This would not have been a problem for them," said Azman.

Another theory mooted by dealers for the sharp rise in Tenaga's share price this week was that local pension and savings funds were actively buying Tenaga stock as a show of confidence in the company's new chief executive officer, Tajudin Ali.
"It could be a political move," said one analyst.
